articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: NACZ, Lotteries Board turn to skits to champion responsible gambling
more.description: Mbulelo Mpofu, mbulelo.smpofu@gmail.com THE country’s arts watchdog, the National Arts Council of Zimbabwe (NACZ), has partnered with the Lotteries and Gaming Board to harness the power of creative storytelling in promoting responsible gambling through the Responsible Gambling Skit Challenge. The initiative, which combines entertainment with public education, is calling on Zimbabwean skit makers to use their creativity and digital platforms to communicate the importance of making informed and responsible choices when engaging in gambling activities. Under the challenge, creatives are being invited to produce a one- to two-minute skit centred on responsible gambling and share it with the public through Facebook. Participants are required to post their skits on their Facebook pages, tag NACZ and the Lotteries and Gaming Board, and use the hashtag #ResponsibleGambling2026 to officially enter the competition. The campaign comes at a time when social media and short-form video content have become powerful tools for reaching large audiences, particularly young people. By involving skit makers, the organisers are seeking to move beyond conventional awareness campaigns and deliver the responsible gambling message in an entertaining, accessible and relatable manner. The competition’s top prize is US$1 000, with the winner determined by the skit that records the highest number of views and engagement. The deadline for submissions is 31 August, giving creatives several weeks to conceptualise, produce and publish their entries. Beyond the competition and its cash incentive, the initiative places emphasis on the need for members of the public to understand that gambling should remain a form of entertainment rather than become a source of financial dependence. Responsible gambling involves setting limits on the amount of money and time spent gambling and recognising when gambling begins to interfere with an individual’s financial stability, relationships, work or general wellbeing. It also means understanding that gambling outcomes are based on chance and that there is no guaranteed strategy for winning. The NACZ and Lotteries and Gaming Board are therefore using the creative sector as an avenue to make these messages more accessible to the wider public. For skit makers, the challenge also presents an opportunity to demonstrate how comedy, drama and storytelling can be used to address social issues without losing their entertainment value. A well-crafted one- or two-minute production can portray everyday situations, consequences of irresponsible gambling and practical ways of maintaining healthy boundaries. The campaign further highlights the growing role of Zimbabwe’s creative economy in public education. With digital content creators commanding significant audiences on social media, creative campaigns can potentially reach demographics that may not engage with traditional awareness initiatives. The organisers are encouraging participants to think creatively while ensuring that their productions clearly communicate the central message of responsible gambling. The competition also provides an avenue for emerging content creators to gain visibility, with audience engagement forming part of the criteria that will determine the winning entry. The challenge is expected to attract a wide range of comedic and dramatic interpretations of responsible gambling, while placing an important public-interest message at the heart of Zimbabwe’s increasingly influential digital creative space. At its core, the campaign seeks to remind the public that gambling should be approached with caution and self-control. It is not a means of securing guaranteed income, recovering financial losses or solving financial difficulties. The partnership between NACZ and the Lotteries and Gaming Board consequently represents an intersection between regulation, public awareness and the arts, demonstrating how creative expression can be deployed to encourage responsible behaviour and spark conversations around issues affecting communities. - Follow on X @MbuleloMpofu

more.title: Byo to honour goalkeeping great Lucky Dube
more.description: Lovemore Dube lovemore.dube@chronicle.co.zw FORMER Zimbabwe national team goalkeeper Lucky Dube will be remembered next Saturday with a tombstone unveiling ceremony and a football tournament in Bulawayo as family, friends and the football fraternity celebrate the life of one of the country’s most gifted goalkeepers. Dube, who died in 1997 at the age of 34, would have turned 63 on Thursday last week. His widow, Mrs Sekani Dube (née Ntutu), confirmed that the family had organised a day of remembrance beginning with the unveiling of his tombstone in the morning before a social football tournament featuring four teams in Mzilikazi. “I am delighted that we will celebrate his life as family, my two sons with him and their four brothers. The children have come together to arrange the ceremony and we will have football because it was his love and it gave him fame and fortune,” she said. The tournament will feature Wolves of Nguboyenja, Madamara FC, Barbourfields Stars and Mzilikazi United, clubs chosen because Dube grew up in Mzilikazi and interacted closely with young footballers from neighbouring Nguboyenja. Born in Bulawayo, Dube attended Nhlambabaloyi Primary School before completing his Grade Seven education at Mzilikazi High School. He began his football career at Highlanders juniors before joining Bulawayo Wanderers, where his talent quickly became evident. By 1980, he had earned selection into Zimbabwe’s pioneering Under-20 national team shortly after Independence. His performances later earned him a move to Bata Power before joining Dynamos, where he replaced Japhet Mparutsa after the latter moved to Black Rhinos in 1983. During his successful stay in Harare, Dube won several trophies with the Glamour Boys before returning to Bulawayo in 1989. Mrs Dube recalled how she was introduced to football through him. “One day around 1980 when I was still at school, he asked me to accompany him to a football match. My brother Felix played football but I did not care much about the sport. I agreed to accompany him and we found curtain-raisers in action. I did not know Lucky Dube was a football player. “After watching for a while, he excused himself and said he would be back shortly. My jaw dropped when I saw him in football gear starting for Bulawayo Wanderers. The rest is history. He gave me two wonderful sons, Thabo and Nhlanhla. He was a loving man, very sociable and quite smart,” she said. Both sons followed their father into football. Nhlanhla played for Highlanders and Zimbabwe Saints, while Thabo graduated from Rutz Celtics juniors into the club’s Division Two side that later won promotion to Division One. Thabo said growing up as the son of a football legend came with enormous expectations. “I think I speak for all my siblings when I say growing up as a legend’s son was not easy because people expected the same or even better from us. He always reminded us that we had big shoes to fill. “Our father was a legend, the smartest man I have ever known. He was punctual, disciplined and always encouraged us to think outside the box,” he said. Dynamos chairman Vincent Chawonza described Dube as one of the club’s outstanding servants. “Without doubt he is a Dynamos legend and he won a lot with the club. He will always remain in our hearts and Dynamos will participate in the day chosen by his family to remember him,” said Chawonza. Former national team goalkeeper Japhet Mparutsa, who competed with Dube for places in the Under-20 side, recently paid tribute to him on social media. “Lucky Dube was our first-choice goalkeeper. He was tall, gifted, confident and naturally talented. He carried himself with professionalism and pride,” wrote Mparutsa. He said competing with Dube pushed him to improve his own game. “I respected Lucky because he was talented, but I also believed in my own ability and wanted to keep improving. Competing with a talented goalkeeper like him pushed me to become better,” he wrote. Mparutsa would later become the first goalkeeper to win the Soccer Star of the Year award in 1982. Dube and Mparutsa were part of a generation of goalkeepers that included Frank Mkanga, Victor Dliwayo, Posani Sibanda, Mike Mhlanga, Stewart Gilbert, Raphael Phiri, Labani Kandi and Peter Nkomo. Nearly three decades after his death, Dube remains fondly remembered by family, former teammates, supporters and football historians as a talented goalkeeper whose elegance, intelligence and professionalism left a lasting mark on Zimbabwean football.

more.title: Saving vultures through art: Byo creatives answer nature’s call
more.description: Mbulelo Mpofu Sunday Life Reporter THE often-maligned vulture is set to become the unlikely muse for Zimbabwe’s next generation of artists as conservationists turn to creativity to change public perceptions of one of nature’s most misunderstood birds. In commemoration of International Vulture Awareness Day (IVAD) 2026, celebrated annually on the first Saturday of September, BirdLife Zimbabwe’s Matabeleland Branch Committee and the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe have launched an open call inviting artists aged 35 years and below to explore and express the vital ecological role of vultures through visual art under the theme, “Vulture Interactions”. The exhibition will form part of commemorations to be held at the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe in Bulawayo on September 6, bringing together conservationists, artists, young people and members of the public in a united effort to spotlight a species facing an increasingly uncertain future. Paintings, drawings, photos, digital art, mixed media and installations will dress the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe in Bulawayo walls. One of the leaders of the initiative, Mthabisi Bafana Charles Khumalo, curator of the Ornithology Department at the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe and Special Species and Raptors Coordinator for BirdLife Zimbabwe’s Matabeleland Branch Committee, who believes art can become a powerful conservation tool. IVAD has grown into a global campaign dedicated to highlighting the ecological importance of vultures while drawing attention to the urgent need for their protection. The campaign was established to challenge long-held misconceptions surrounding vultures, birds that are frequently associated with death and decay despite playing a critical role in maintaining healthy ecosystems. The first co-ordinated global observance was launched in 2009 by the Hawk Conservancy Trust in the United Kingdom and the Endangered Wildlife Trust in South Africa. Since then, conservation organisations around the world have used the occasion to educate communities, influence policy and promote rescue and rehabilitation initiatives. This year’s Bulawayo commemorations seek to build on that legacy by merging conservation with artistic expression. “Our plan is to drive vulture conservation impact by spreading awareness through a commemoration at the Natural History Museum and an art exhibition with the theme ‘Vulture Interactions’. We want to use the power of art by engaging young creatives (35 years and below) to exhibit their vulture art and inspire the audience in conservation, fulfilling a crucial need to involve youth and shift public perception. “It is a perfect blend of education and community engagement, which is essential for driving behavioural and societal change,” said Khumalo. The initiative comes against the backdrop of an alarming decline in Zimbabwe’s vulture populations. Of the 11 vulture species found across Africa, six occur in Zimbabwe, with all but one listed as threatened or endangered. Among the most imperilled are the white-backed vulture, white-headed vulture and hooded vulture, all of which are classified as Critically Endangered. Conservationists warn that the disappearance of these scavengers would have devastating consequences not only for biodiversity, but also for public health and the economy. Poisoning remains the single greatest threat. Poachers frequently lace animal carcasses with poison to eliminate vultures whose circling flight patterns can expose illegal hunting activities to wildlife authorities. These incidents often result in catastrophic losses, including the poisoning of 191 vultures in Gonarezhou National Park in 2012 and another 94 birds near the park’s boundary in 2017. Accidental poisonings are also widespread, particularly in farming communities where poisoned carcasses intended to kill predators such as lions and hyenas are later consumed by vultures. Another major challenge is belief-based use, where vultures are killed for body parts believed to possess supernatural powers for use in traditional medicine. Across Africa, this practice accounts for an estimated 27 percent of threats facing vultures. To address the issue, BirdLife Zimbabwe has partnered with the Zimbabwe National Traditional Healers’ Association (Zinatha), whose members have pledged to identify sustainable alternatives to the use of vulture parts in traditional healing practices. Habitat destruction presents another growing concern. Illegal farming and land-use changes continue to reduce nesting and feeding habitats, while a 2025 Nasa study highlighted the impact of drought and elephant damage on vegetation surrounding waterholes, threatening the nesting trees used by white-backed vultures. Electrocutions and collisions with power lines further compound the pressures facing already declining populations. Despite their often negative reputation, vultures perform one of nature’s most essential ecological services. Often referred to as nature’s clean-up crew, they rapidly dispose of animal carcasses before they become breeding grounds for dangerous diseases. Their uniquely acidic digestive systems enable them to consume pathogens such as anthrax and rabies without becoming infected, effectively preventing the spread of diseases to livestock, wildlife and people. The economic contribution of this natural sanitation service is equally remarkable. Studies estimate that vultures save Zimbabwe more than US$1 million annually through free waste disposal services that would otherwise require costly human intervention. A former Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority (ZimParks) director once estimated that a single vulture provides ecosystem services worth more than US$11 000 during its lifetime. International research has also illustrated the consequences of vulture declines. In India, the collapse of vulture populations triggered an explosion in feral dog numbers and contributed to tens of thousands of additional rabies-related deaths. Researchers are now investigating whether Zimbabwe’s recent anthrax outbreaks may similarly be linked to declining vulture populations. Khumalo believes the Bulawayo commemorations represent an important contribution to Zimbabwe’s broader conservation strategy. “Our event directly supports the long-term survival of these critically important birds by educating the public, engaging the next generation of conservationists, and celebrating the misunderstood, yet essential, vulture,” he said. The programme brings together BirdLife Zimbabwe’s Matabeleland Branch, the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe’s Ornithology Department and the Conservation Sisters Connect programme under Wildlife Conservation Action. The partnership seeks to combine scientific expertise, youth engagement and artistic expression while strengthening conservation leadership among young Zimbabweans, particularly women. Conservation Sisters Connect is a fellowship programme that equips young women with practical conservation skills and mentorship, helping build a stronger future generation of environmental leaders. The commemorations also complement BirdLife Zimbabwe’s wider conservation efforts under the Zimbabwe Vulture Action Plan, developed jointly with ZimParks and other stakeholders. As the lead co-ordinator of the national strategy, BirdLife Zimbabwe oversees the Vulture Working Group, which brings together government agencies, researchers and non-governmental organisations to coordinate conservation interventions. Its work ranges from establishing Vulture Safe Zones and community-based Vulture Support Groups to deploying satellite tracking technology, in partnership with IFAW and ZimParks, to monitor bird movements and identify poaching hotspots. The organisation also continues advocating for stronger wildlife protection laws while expanding community education programmes across the country. By inviting young artists to interpret the theme, “Vulture Interactions”, organisers hope creativity will become a catalyst for changing attitudes towards birds that have for generations been unfairly associated with superstition and death. Instead, the exhibition seeks to present vultures for what they truly are - silent custodians of ecosystem health whose survival is inseparable from that of Zimbabwe’s wildlife, landscapes and communities. IVAD approaches, conservationists are hopeful that brushes, canvases and imagination will succeed where fear and misunderstanding have long prevailed, giving Zimbabwe’s embattled vultures a renewed voice through the language of art. – Follow on X @MbuleloMpofu
